proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(n_{i,T}\) be the integer count assigned to arm \(i\) by \(\text{def:static-comparator}\).  Largest-remainder rounding gives
\[
 \frac{n_{i,T}}{T}\longrightarrow w_i>0.
\]
Under \(\text{ass:gaussian-marginals}\) and \(\text{ass:independent-streams}\), for every \(j\ne h\),
\[
 D_{j,T}:=\overline Y_{j,T}-\overline Y_{h,T}
 \sim \mathcal N\!\left(-\Delta_j,\frac{s_j}{n_{j,T}}+\frac{s_h}{n_{h,T}}\right).
\]
Put \(a_{j,T}=T(s_j/n_{j,T}+s_h/n_{h,T})\).  Then \(a_{j,T}\to v_j+v_h\).  If \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), the Chernoff calculation
\[
 \mathbb P(Z\ge x)\le \inf_{\lambda>0}e^{-\lambda x+\lambda^2/2}=e^{-x^2/2}
\]
and, for \(x\ge1\), integration of the Gaussian density on \([x,x+x^{-1}]\), give
\[
 \frac{e^{-(x+x^{-1})^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,x}
 \le \mathbb P(Z\ge x)\le e^{-x^2/2}.
\]
Taking \(x=\sqrt T\,\Delta_j/\sqrt{a_{j,T}}\) therefore yields
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}-\frac1T\log\mathbb P(D_{j,T}\ge0)
 =\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}.
\]
The positivity \(\Delta_j>0\) used here is exactly \(\text{ass:unique-best}\).  Gaussian ties have probability zero.  Hence the static empirical-best error event is the finite union of the events \(\{D_{j,T}>0\}\), and
\[
 \max_{j\ne h}\mathbb P(D_{j,T}>0)
 \le \mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\mathrm{stat}}(\widehat h_T^{\mathrm{stat}}\ne h)
 \le \sum_{j\ne h}\mathbb P(D_{j,T}>0).
\]
Taking logarithms, dividing by \(T\), and using that the number \(K-1\) of terms is fixed proves
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\mathrm{stat}}(\widehat h_T^{\mathrm{stat}}\ne h)
 =\min_{j\ne h}\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}=I_w(\mu).
\]

We first establish directly the finite-dimensional Gaussian fact needed below.  Fix a positive integer \(d\), positive numbers \(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_d\), and let \(X_T=(X_{\ell,T})_{\ell=1}^d\) have independent coordinates
\[
 X_{\ell,T}\sim\mathcal N\!\left(m_\ell,\frac{\tau_\ell}{T\alpha_{\ell,T}}\right),
 \qquad \alpha_{\ell,T}\longrightarrow\alpha_\ell>0,
\]
and define
\[
 J_T(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d\frac{\alpha_{\ell,T}(x_\ell-m_\ell)^2}{2\tau_\ell},
 \qquad
 J(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d\frac{\alpha_\ell(x_\ell-m_\ell)^2}{2\tau_\ell}.
\]
Suppose \(P_T\) is a closed polyhedron whose finitely many affine defining coefficients converge to those of a closed polyhedron \(P\), and suppose \(P\) has a strictly feasible point.  Then
\[
 \inf_{P_T}J_T\longrightarrow\inf_PJ. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, uniform positivity of the \(\alpha_{\ell,T}\) makes \(J_T\) uniformly coercive.  Thus minimizers are bounded.  Every convergent subsequence of minimizers has a limit in \(P\), by convergence of the inequalities, and its limiting objective is at least \(\inf_PJ\).  Conversely, mix any point of \(P\) with a strictly feasible point.  The mixture is strictly feasible, converges back to the original point, and belongs to \(P_T\) for all sufficiently large \(T\).  Continuity of \(J_T\) gives the reverse inequality in (1).

For completeness, this also gives the exact logarithmic probability.  After whitening, the squared Euclidean distance from the origin to the transformed closed convex set is \(2T\inf_{P_T}J_T\).  If \(p_T\) is its Euclidean projection, the projection inequality places that set in the half-space \(\{z:p_T^{\mathsf T}z\ge\lVert p_T\rVert^2\}\).  For a standard Gaussian vector \(Z\), optimizing \(\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda p_T^{\mathsf T}Z\}\exp\{-\lambda\lVert p_T\rVert^2\}\) over \(\lambda>0\) gives
\[
 \mathbb P(X_T\in P_T)\le \exp\{-T\inf_{P_T}J_T\}. \tag{2}
\]
If the mean belongs to the set, the right side of (2) is one and the same conclusion holds.  For the reverse logarithmic inequality, choose a strictly feasible \(y\in P\) with \(J(y)\le\inf_PJ+\varepsilon\).  Such a \(y\) exists by mixing a minimizer with a strictly feasible point.  A sufficiently small fixed ball about \(y\) lies in \(P_T\) for all large \(T\).  Integrating the product Gaussian density over this ball yields
\[
 \limsup_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P(X_T\in\operatorname{int}P_T)
 \le \sup_{x\text{ in the ball}}J(x)\le \inf_PJ+2\varepsilon,
\]
where the logarithm of the Gaussian normalizing factor is \(O(\log T)=o(T)\), and the ball may be chosen so that the last inequality holds.  Combining this with (1)--(2) and then letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P(X_T\in\operatorname{int}P_T)=\inf_PJ. \tag{3}
\]
The same mixing argument proves at the same time that the infimum over \(P\) equals the infimum over its strict interior.

We apply (3) to the design in \(\text{def:proportional-design}\).  Pre-sampling the mutually independent streams, as in \(\text{ass:independent-streams}\), means that on a putative branch \(e\) the first-batch means \(x_i\) and the fresh second-batch means \(z_i\), \(i\ne e\), may be considered jointly without conditioning on which arm is eliminated.  Their product Gaussian density has, at speed \(T\), the rate
\[
 R_{T,e}(x,z;\mu)
 =\sum_i\frac{(N_{i,T}^{(1)}/T)(x_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}
 +\sum_{i\ne e}\frac{(N_{i,T}^{(2)}(e)/T)(z_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}.
\]
Largest-remainder rounding has bounded coordinate error, so
\[
 N_{i,T}^{(1)}/T\to q_i(\rho),
 \qquad N_{i,T}^{(2)}(e)/T\to r_i(e;\rho),
\]
and every limiting coefficient appearing in this branch is positive.  Thus \(R_{T,e}\to R_e\) coefficientwise and uniformly on compact sets.

Because all Gaussian ties have probability zero, arm \(e\) is eliminated precisely, up to a null set, on the strict cone
\[
 x_e<x_i\quad(i\ne e).
\]
If \(e=h\), this event itself forces a wrong deployment.  Formula (3), with the closed cone \(\mathcal B_h\), gives its exponent
\[
 Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)
 =\inf_{x\in\mathcal B_h}\sum_i\frac{q_i(\rho)(x_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}.
\]
The second-batch coordinates integrate out in this branch.  If \(e\ne h\), a wrong deployment occurs exactly when at least one \(j\ne e,h\) satisfies, again up to a null tie event,
\[
 m_j(e;x,z)>m_h(e;x,z).
\]
For fixed \((e,j)\), adjoining the weak version of this inequality to \(x\in\mathcal B_e\) gives precisely the closed polyhedron in \(\text{def:branch-programs}\), hence (3) gives exponent \(Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)\).  Every one of these polyhedra has a strict point: take \(x_e\) below all other first-batch coordinates and, for a terminal branch, increase \(z_j\) until the terminal inequality is strict.  Convex mixing with that point proves explicitly that its closed and strict-interior infima agree.

The error event is the union of the one best-elimination event and the \((K-1)(K-2)\) terminal events just described.  For any fixed finite family \((A_{\ell,T})\),
\[
 \max_\ell\mathbb P(A_{\ell,T})
 \le \mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_\ell A_{\ell,T}\right)
 \le \sum_\ell\mathbb P(A_{\ell,T}),
\]
so (3) makes the exponent of the union the minimum of the branch exponents.  Consequently the defining limit exists and
\[
 \Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)
 =\min\left\{Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu),
 \min_{e\ne h}\min_{j\ne e,h}Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)\right\}.
\]
Finally, the coercivity and strict-feasibility argument proving (1), applied to the rounded coefficients and to the convergent aggregate-mean coefficients, shows that every rounded branch value converges to its displayed ideal-proportion value.  Hence deterministic largest-remainder rounding leaves this limit unchanged.

By \(q_i(\rho)=\rho w_i\), the best-elimination program in \(\text{def:branch-programs}\) factors as
\[
 Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)=\rho E_h(\mu),\qquad
 E_h(\mu):=\inf_{x_h\le x_j\ (j\ne h)}
 \sum_i\frac{(x_i-\mu_i)^2}{2v_i}. \tag{4}
\]
Translate all means and optimization coordinates by \(-\mu_h\), so that \(\mu_h=0\) and \(\mu_j=-\Delta_j\).  Fixing \(x_h=-t\), projection of \(-\Delta_j\) onto the half-line \([-t,\infty)\) gives \(x_j=\max\{-\Delta_j,-t\}\).  The resulting objective is
\[
 \frac{t^2}{2v_h}+\sum_{j\ne h}\frac{(\Delta_j-t)_+^2}{2v_j}. \tag{5}
\]
For \(t<0\), every positive-part term is active and the derivative of (5) is
\[
 \frac{t}{v_h}+\sum_{j\ne h}\frac{t-\Delta_j}{v_j}<0,
\]
using \(\Delta_j>0\) from \(\text{ass:unique-best}\).  Thus no minimizer has \(t<0\), and (4)--(5) give an exact one-dimensional representation over \(t\ge0\).

Let \(I=I_w(\mu)>0\), whose value is established in \(\text{lem:static-exponent}\).  Its definition implies
\[
 \Delta_j\ge \sqrt I\,d_{hj}\qquad(j\ne h).
\]
Substitute \(t=\sqrt I\,u\) in (5) and use monotonicity of \((a-u)_+^2\) in \(a\).  Then
\[
 E_h(\mu)
 \ge I\min_{u\ge0}\left\{\frac{u^2}{2v_h}
 +\sum_{j\ne h}\frac{(d_{hj}-u)_+^2}{2v_j}\right\}
 =I C_h(v).
\]
Together with (4), this is the asserted bound.  If \(\mu_h=0\) and \(\mu_j=-d_{hj}\), every pairwise static exponent is one, so \(I_w(\mu)=1\), and (5) is exactly \(F_h\).  Equality follows.

It remains to prove strictness and the computation claim.  Fix one \(j\ne h\) and put
\[
 f_j(t)=\frac{t^2}{2v_h}+\frac{(d_{hj}-t)_+^2}{2v_j}.
\]
On \([0,d_{hj}]\), its unique minimizer is
\[
 t_j=\frac{v_h}{v_h+v_j}d_{hj},
 \qquad f_j(t_j)=\frac{d_{hj}^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}=1,
\]
while on \([d_{hj},\infty)\) it is strictly larger than one.  Hence \(F_h(t)\ge f_j(t)\ge1\).  The continuous coercive function \(F_h\) attains its minimum.  If that minimum were one, its minimizer would have to equal \(t_j\) and every other summand would have to vanish.  Since \(K\ge3\), choose \(k\ne h,j\).  But
\[
 t_j=\frac{\sqrt2\,v_h}{\sqrt{v_h+v_j}}
 <\sqrt{2v_h}<\sqrt{2(v_h+v_k)}=d_{hk},
\]
so the \(k\)-summand is strictly positive, a contradiction.  Therefore \(C_h(v)>1\).

Finally, after sorting the \(K-1\) numbers \(d_{hj}\), the active set \(A=\{j:d_{hj}>t\}\) is constant on each of the resulting \(K\) intervals.  On such an interval the derivative is
\[
 \frac{t}{v_h}+\sum_{j\in A}\frac{t-d_{hj}}{v_j},
\]
whose zero is
\[
 t_A=\frac{\sum_{j\in A}d_{hj}/v_j}{1/v_h+\sum_{j\in A}1/v_j}.
\]
Convexity says that the minimum on the interval is obtained by clipping \(t_A\) to that interval.  Evaluating these at most \(K\) candidates and taking the smallest value computes \(C_h\).

First, the allocation in \(\text{def:static-comparator}\) is well defined for every finite positive \(s\).  Extend its maximin objective continuously to the closed simplex by assigning value zero when a coordinate vanishes.  It is positive at the uniform allocation and zero on the boundary; hence a maximizer exists and lies in \(\mathcal W\).  Thus every \(w_i\), and consequently every \(v_i=s_i/w_i\), is finite and positive.  This uses \(\text{ass:known-variances}\) only to make the resulting design selectable before observing rewards.

For a branch \(e\) on which \(h\) survives, \(\text{def:proportional-design}\) gives, for every \(i\ne e\),
\[
 n_i(e;\rho)=\rho w_i+\frac{(1-\rho)w_i}{1-w_e}
 =c_e(\rho)w_i,
 \qquad
 c_e(\rho):=1+(1-\rho)\frac{w_e}{1-w_e}. \tag{6}
\]
Drop the elimination inequalities from the program \(Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}\), retain only coordinates \(h,j\), and fix an aggregate value \(y_i\) for either retained arm.  Weighted least squares gives
\[
 \inf_{q_i x_i+r_i z_i=n_i y_i}
 \left\{\frac{q_i(x_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}
 +\frac{r_i(z_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}\right\}
 =\frac{n_i(y_i-\mu_i)^2}{2s_i}; \tag{7}
\]
indeed, the Lagrange equations set \(x_i=z_i=y_i\).  Minimizing the sum of (7) for \(i=h,j\) under \(y_j\ge y_h\) puts the optimum on \(y_j=y_h\) and yields
\[
 Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)
 \ge \frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(s_h/n_h+s_j/n_j)}
 =c_e(\rho)\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}
 \ge c_e(\rho)I_w(\mu). \tag{8}
\]
No conditioning on the branch has been used; (8) follows by relaxing its unconditional convex program.

The lemma \(\text{lem:weighted-projection}\) gives
\[
 Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)\ge \rho C_h(v)I_w(\mu)\ge \rho C(v)I_w(\mu). \tag{9}
\]
Combining (8)--(9) with the exact branch formula in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) proves, for every \(0<\rho<1\),
\[
 \Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)
 \ge \min\{\rho C,\,1+(1-\rho)\eta\}I_w(\mu). \tag{10}
\]
The strict projection result gives \(C>1\), while interiority of \(w\) gives \(\eta>0\).  Consequently
\[
 \rho^\star=\frac{1+\eta}{C+\eta}<1,
 \qquad
 \rho^\star-\frac1C
 =\frac{\eta(C-1)}{C(C+\eta)}>0.
\]
At this value the two quantities in (10) agree:
\[
 \rho^\star C=1+(1-\rho^\star)\eta
 =\frac{C(1+\eta)}{C+\eta}=G.
\]
Moreover
\[
 G-1=\frac{\eta(C-1)}{C+\eta}>0.
\]
Since \(I_w(\mu)>0\) under \(\text{ass:unique-best}\), (10) proves
\[
 \Gamma_{\rho^\star,w}(\mu)\ge G I_w(\mu)>I_w(\mu)
\]
for every unique-best \(\mu\) and every finite positive variance vector \(s\).

For any \(e\ne h\), the survivor fractions in \(\text{def:proportional-design}\) satisfy
\[
 n_i(e;\rho)=c_e(\rho)w_i,
 \qquad c_e(\rho)=1+(1-\rho)\frac{w_e}{1-w_e}.
\]
Dropping the elimination inequalities in a terminal program and minimizing first- and second-batch quadratic costs subject to a fixed aggregate mean sets the two batch means equal.  The remaining two-arm projection therefore gives
\[
 Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)
 \ge c_e(\rho)\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}
 \ge c_e(\rho)I_w(\mu).
\]
Together with \(Q_h^{\mathrm E}\ge\rho C_h I_w\) from \(\text{lem:weighted-projection}\) and the branch minimum in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\), this gives, for every \(0<\rho<1\),
\[
 \frac{\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}
 \ge L(\rho):=\min\{\rho C,\,1+(1-\rho)\eta\} \tag{11}
\]
for every unique-best \(\mu\).

We now construct matching witnesses.  Choose \(h_0\in\arg\min_h C_h\), set \(\mu_{h_0}=0\), and set \(\mu_j=-d_{h_0j}\) for \(j\ne h_0\).  The equality part of \(\text{lem:weighted-projection}\) gives \(I_w(\mu)=1\) and
\[
 Q_{h_0}^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)=\rho C_{h_0}=\rho C.
\]
The exact branch minimum in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) therefore implies
\[
 \inf_{\mu:\,|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}
 \frac{\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}\le \rho C. \tag{12}
\]

For the other branch, choose \(e_0\in\arg\min_e w_e/(1-w_e)\).  Since \(K\ge3\), choose two distinct survivors \(h,j\in\mathcal A\setminus\{e_0\}\).  Put
\[
 \mu_h=0,\qquad \mu_j=-d_{hj},\qquad
 \mu_{e_0}=-2M,\qquad
 \mu_k=-M\quad(k\notin\{h,j,e_0\}), \tag{13}
\]
where \(M\) is sufficiently large.  In particular, choose it so that all pairwise static exponents involving a member of \(\mathcal A\setminus\{h,j\}\) are at least one.  Then \(h\) is unique best and \(I_w(\mu)=1\), with equality supplied by the pair \((h,j)\).

If the elimination constraints are omitted from the \((e_0,j)\) terminal program, (7) shows that its value is
\[
 c_{e_0}(\rho)\frac{d_{hj}^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}=c_{e_0}(\rho).
\]
The unique minimizing aggregate means for \(h,j\) coincide at the finite value
\[
 y=\frac{\mu_h/v_h+\mu_j/v_j}{1/v_h+1/v_j},
\]
and equality in (7) takes \(x_h=z_h=x_j=z_j=y\).  Every unrelated survivor remains at its mean, while \(x_{e_0}=\mu_{e_0}=-2M\).  For all sufficiently large \(M\), this point satisfies \(x_{e_0}<x_i\) for every \(i\ne e_0\).  Hence the elimination constraints are inactive at the unconstrained optimizer and
\[
 Q_{e_0,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)=c_{e_0}(\rho)
 =1+(1-\rho)\eta. \tag{14}
\]
The exact branch formula consequently gives the second upper bound on the infimum.  Combining (11)--(14) proves
\[
 \inf_{\mu:\,|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}
 \frac{\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}
 =\min\{\rho C,\,1+(1-\rho)\eta\}.
\]
More precisely, the first witness attains the worst ratio whenever \(\rho C\le1+(1-\rho)\eta\), and the terminal witness attains it under the reverse inequality; each witness always attains its named branch value.

The first affine function is strictly increasing and the second is strictly decreasing on \((0,1)\).  Their unique intersection is
\[
 \rho=\frac{1+\eta}{C+\eta}=\rho^\star,
\]
which lies in \((0,1)\) by \(C>1\) and \(\eta>0\).  Therefore it is the unique maximizer of their minimum, and the maximum equals \(\rho^\star C=G\).

Write \(r=\sqrt2\).  Maximizing the static pair criterion is equivalent to minimizing
\[
 M(u)=\max_{i<j}\left(\frac{s_i}{u_i}+\frac{s_j}{u_j}\right)
\]
over the simplex.  For an arbitrary allocation let \(a=u_1+u_2\).  One of \(u_1,u_2\) is at most \(a/2\); pairing that arm with arm \(3\) gives
\[
 M(u)\ge \frac2a+\frac4{1-a}. \tag{15}
\]
The right side has its unique minimum at \(1-a=\sqrt2a\), namely \(a=r-1\).  At
\[
 w_1=w_2=\frac{r-1}{2},\qquad w_3=2-r,
\]
equality holds in (15), and the remaining pair value \(2/w_1=4/a\) is smaller because \(a>1/3\).  Thus this allocation globally minimizes \(M\), and the lexicographic selector in \(\text{def:static-comparator}\) returns it.

The corresponding unit-horizon variances are
\[
 v_1=v_2=2+2r=:a_0,\qquad v_3=4+2r=:b_0,
\]
and
\[
 d_{31}=d_{32}=\sqrt{2(a_0+b_0)}=a_0.
\]
For \(h=3\), both competitor terms are active at the stationary point
\[
 t_3=\frac{2a_0b_0}{a_0+2b_0}=\frac{8+12r}{7}\in(0,a_0).
\]
Direct substitution gives
\[
 C_3=\frac{t_3^2}{2b_0}+\frac{(a_0-t_3)^2}{a_0}
 =\frac{6+2r}{7}. \tag{16}
\]
To verify that this is the active coefficient, consider \(h=1\); the case \(h=2\) is symmetric.  Here \(d_{12}=2\sqrt{a_0}<d_{13}=a_0\).  Therefore, for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
 F_1(t)\ge H(t):=\frac{t^2}{2a_0}
 +(d_{12}-t)_+^2\left(\frac1{2a_0}+\frac1{2b_0}\right).
\]
The unique minimum of \(H\) equals
\[
 \frac{2(1/a_0+1/b_0)}{2/a_0+1/b_0}=\frac{6+2r}{7}=C_3.
\]
At the minimizer of \(H\), the strict inequality \(d_{13}>d_{12}>t\) makes \(F_1(t)>H(t)\).  Since both functions are continuous and coercive, equality of their minima would force equality at that unique minimizer, which is impossible.  Thus \(C_1=C_2>C_3\), and (16) gives \(C=C_3\).

The least survivor expansion is attained by arm \(1\) or \(2\):
\[
 \eta=\frac{w_1}{1-w_1}=\frac{r-1}{3-r}=\frac{2r-1}{7},
\]
whereas \(w_3/(1-w_3)>1\).  Substitution in \(\text{def:robust-schedule}\) now gives
\[
 \rho^\star=2r-2,
 \qquad
 G=\rho^\star C=\frac{8r-4}{7}. \tag{17}
\]

We finally verify both coupled witnesses exactly.  For the best-elimination witness take
\[
 \mu_3=0,\qquad \mu_1=\mu_2=-a_0.
\]
For this paragraph put
\[
 c_e:=1+(1-\rho^\star)\frac{w_e}{1-w_e}.
\]
Then \(I_w=1\), and the one-dimensional projection above gives \(Q_3^{\mathrm E}=\rho^\star C_3=G\).  For every surviving-best terminal branch, dropping the elimination inequalities and minimizing the two batch costs at a fixed aggregate mean sets the two batch means equal.  The resulting two-arm projection gives
\[
 Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}\ge c_e\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_3+v_j)}\ge c_e I_w\ge G,
\]
because at \(\rho^\star\), \(\min_e c_e=G\).  The exact branch formula in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) therefore gives \(\Gamma_{\rho^\star,w}=G I_w\).

For the terminal witness eliminate arm \(1\), retain best arm \(3\) and challenger \(2\), and take
\[
 \mu_3=0,\qquad \mu_2=-a_0,\qquad \mu_1=-2M,\qquad M>a_0/2.
\]
Again \(I_w=1\).  The unconstrained terminal optimizer has \(x_2=z_2=x_3=z_3=y\), where
\[
 y=-\frac{a_0b_0}{a_0+b_0},
\]
and \(x_1=-2M<y\).  Thus arm \(1\) is strictly the first-batch loser at this optimizer, so the coupled branch constraint is inactive and
\[
 Q_{1,2}^{\mathrm T}=c_1(\rho^\star)=1+(1-\rho^\star)\eta=G.
\]
For the terminal witness, direct minimization of the best-elimination program after fixing \(x_3=-t\) gives
\[
 Q_3^{\mathrm E}=\rho^\star\min_{t\ge0}
 \left\{\frac{t^2}{2v_3}+\sum_{k\ne3}\frac{(\Delta_k-t)_+^2}{2v_k}\right\}
 \ge \rho^\star C_3 I_w=G I_w.
\]
The same batch-aggregation calculation in the preceding paragraph gives every terminal branch a value at least \(c_e I_w\ge G I_w\), while the \((1,2)\) branch is exactly \(G I_w\).  Hence the terminal witness also has adaptive exponent \(G I_w\), completing the exact radical stress test.

Fix a budget for which every prescribed positive count is at least one.  On the event that \(h\) is eliminated, the vector of first-batch means is Gaussian with independent coordinates and the closed weak-error cone is \(\mathcal B_h\).  Whitening this vector, projecting the origin onto the whitened cone, and applying the supporting-half-space Chernoff argument (2) from \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) gives
\[
 \mathbb P(h\text{ is eliminated})\le \exp\{-TQ_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\}. \tag{18}
\]
This is an upper bound for the actual strict event because Gaussian ties have probability zero.

For \(e\ne h\) and \(j\ne e,h\), use the independent pre-sampled streams from \(\text{ass:independent-streams}\) and form jointly the first-batch means and the fresh second-batch means prescribed for branch \(e\).  Their exact finite-budget Gaussian quadratic rate is \(T\) times the rounded program in \(\text{def:finite-certificate}\).  The joint event that \(e\) is the first-batch loser and that the aggregate mean of \(j\) is at least that of \(h\) is contained in its closed branch polyhedron.  The same projection and scalar Chernoff calculation therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb P(e\text{ is eliminated and }j\text{ terminally beats }h)
 \le \exp\{-TQ_{T,e,j}^{\mathrm T}\}. \tag{19}
\]
Crucially, (19) is unconditional; it does not replace the first-batch distribution by a distribution conditioned on elimination.

The deployment error is contained in the union of the event in (18) and the events in (19).  There is one term of the first kind.  There are \(K-1\) choices of \(e\ne h\) and, for each, \(K-2\) choices of \(j\ne e,h\).  The union bound and the definition of \(B_T\) thus prove
\[
 \mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\rho,w}(\widehat h_T\ne h)
 \le \exp\{-TQ_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\}
 +\sum_{e\ne h}\sum_{j\ne e,h}\exp\{-TQ_{T,e,j}^{\mathrm T}\}
 =B_T(\mu,s,\rho,w).
\]

Largest-remainder rounding gives coefficientwise convergence of every rounded program.  The equicoercivity and strict-feasibility argument (1) in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) yields
\[
 Q_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\to Q_h^{\mathrm E},
 \qquad Q_{T,e,j}^{\mathrm T}\to Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}.
\]
For a fixed finite collection of real numbers \(a_{\ell,T}\),
\[
 \min_\ell a_{\ell,T}-\frac{\log L}{T}
 \le -\frac1T\log\sum_{\ell=1}^L e^{-Ta_{\ell,T}}
 \le \min_\ell a_{\ell,T}.
\]
Here \(L=1+(K-1)(K-2)\).  Taking limits and invoking the exact branch equality in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) proves
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log B_T(\mu,s,\rho,w)
 =\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu).
\]

Suppose \(s_i=\sigma^2\) for all \(i\).  Let \(u_{(1)}\le u_{(2)}\) be the two smallest coordinates of an arbitrary interior allocation.  Their sum is at most \(2/K\), and therefore
\[
 \max_{i<j}\sigma^2\left(\frac1{u_i}+\frac1{u_j}\right)
 \ge \sigma^2\left(\frac1{u_{(1)}}+\frac1{u_{(2)}}\right)
 \ge \frac{4\sigma^2}{u_{(1)}+u_{(2)}}\ge2K\sigma^2. \tag{20}
\]
The uniform allocation attains (20).  Equality requires \(u_{(1)}=u_{(2)}=1/K\); since these are the two smallest coordinates and all coordinates sum to one, every coordinate must then be \(1/K\).  Hence the selector in \(\text{def:static-comparator}\) has
\[
 w_i=\frac1K,\qquad v_i=K\sigma^2=:V.
\]
Thus \(d_{hj}=2\sqrt V\) for every \(j\ne h\), and
\[
 F_h(t)=\frac{t^2}{2V}+\frac{K-1}{2V}(2\sqrt V-t)_+^2.
\]
Its minimizer is \(t=2(K-1)\sqrt V/K<2\sqrt V\), and direct substitution gives
\[
 C_h=C=\frac{2(K-1)}K.
\]
Also
\[
 \eta=\frac{1/K}{1-1/K}=\frac1{K-1}.
\]
Substitution into \(\text{def:robust-schedule}\) yields
\[
 \rho^\star
 =\frac{K^2}{2(K-1)^2+K},
 \qquad
 G=\frac{2K(K-1)}{2(K-1)^2+K}.
\]
The strict dominance conclusion follows from \(\text{thm:universal-dominance}\).  At \(K=3\), the formulas reduce to \(\rho^\star=9/11\) and \(G=12/11\).

open_obligations.what_is_open: A matching upper saddle bound, and hence the exact unrestricted robust multiplier and an attaining nonproportional-or-proportional design, remain open.
open_obligations.obstruction: The frozen handle specifies neither a compact closed feasible allocation set nor a dual minimax interchange theorem. The branchwise quadratic formula is explicit for each fixed design, but its infimum over all unique-best mean vectors is coupled across elimination branches, and no common dual witness presently bounds every nonproportional first-stage and survivor allocation by the proportional value.
open_obligations.attempted: Reduced every fixed design to unconditional Gaussian polyhedral programs and tested the proportional elimination and terminal witnesses. Those witnesses certify the proportional subclass but do not upper-bound arbitrary branch-specific survivor allocations; optimizing a witness separately after seeing each branch fails to produce one mean vector that is adversarial for the whole unrestricted design.
open_obligations.partial_result:
Because \(\mathfrak D_2\subseteq\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}\), the proved proportional design is feasible for the unrestricted problem, and therefore
\[
 \sup_{D\in\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}}\inf_{\mu:\,|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}
 \frac{\Gamma_D(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}\ge G.
\]
For every fixed two-batch design whose first-stage and branch-specific survivor fractions are specified, the unconditional Gaussian-polyhedron argument in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-exponent}\) also reduces its error exponent to a finite minimum of explicit convex quadratic programs.  What remains unresolved is the matching upper saddle bound after optimizing those programs jointly over all nonproportional allocations.
